title: Detecting Syntactic Change with Pre-trained Transformer Models

source_record_provenance.record_title: Detecting Syntactic Change with Pre-trained Transformer Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses Transformer-based language models (BERT) and empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge in LMs, e.g., syntax-only experiments and POS tagging using BERT embeddings.

It demonstrates that a Transformer model can distinguish syntactic differences across time periods even when semantic information is masked, achieving high accuracy (e.g., 98.6% in era-classification after syntax-focused training).

It trains era-specific POS-taggers based on BERT representations (1830s vs 1990s) and reports high tagging accuracy (1990s model: 97.6% with CoreNLP, 97.2% with CoreNLP for the 1830s model; 98.4% and 98.0% respectively when using Trankit tags), providing concrete empirical evidence of syntactic knowledge in LMs.
It identifies specific instances of syntactic change by comparing predictions from era-specific taggers and by masking target words, enabling direct evidence of syntax-related differences and change.

It grounds the analysis in an actual historical corpus (British Hansard 1830s vs 1990s) and includes multiple validation steps (manual review of top candidates, comparison with Trankit-based tagging, and progressive construction analysis).
triggered_exclusion_points: No exclusion criteria from the original Stage 2 criteria are triggered; the paper remains a direct topical evidence-base on syntactic knowledge in Transformer models.
uncertain_points: The Stage 2 criteria emphasize interpretability research on syntactic knowledge; while the paper analyzes syntactic representations and their behavior in BERT, its framing is oriented toward syntactic change detection rather than a broad interpretability survey. This is unlikely to undermine core status, but could be viewed as a specialized interpretability/application study.

Manual evaluation of the changed-word candidates was conducted by a single author, which may limit generalizability of the qualitative assessments; recall of syntactic-change detection is not objectively quantified due to lack of universal criteria.
evidence_highlights: Transformer-based LMs are shown to encode syntactic information that can be probed by syntax-focused tasks (e.g., masking semantics to force reliance on syntax).
Two era-specific POS-tagging models (1830s and 1990s) trained on BERT representations achieve high tagging accuracy, indicating robust syntactic representations across time periods.

Disagreement-based and masking-based methods identify candidate words that underwent syntactic change, with manual verification showing substantial proportion of true changes among top candidates (7/20 and 11/20 respectively).

Automatic evaluation with Trankit-based tagging corroborates the identification methods, with 35 changed words in the masking method vs 20 in the disagreement method among top 100 candidates, and 75% alignment with human judgments.
The approach detects known syntactic shifts (e.g., rise of progressive constructions), demonstrating the model’s sensitivity to historical syntactic variation.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: This paper directly investigates syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models (BERT) through empirical, syntax-focused experiments and analyses. It uses era-specific model training, syntax-only inputs, and POS-tagging of embeddings to reveal how syntactic information is encoded and how it manifests in predictions, including detection of historical syntactic change. The full text provides multiple clear lines of evidence (high era-classification accuracy with syntax-only input, high POS-tagging accuracy using era-specific embeddings, and filtration-based identification of changed words with manual validation). There is no indication that the work focuses on non-transformer architectures, lacks empirical content, or falls into background/protocol categories. Therefore, the candidate is judged as core for Stage 2 under the original criteria, with strong supporting evidence across multiple independent analyses.

evidence_highlights: Abstract: the paper studies feature interactions in interpretability, trains models to perfection on a formal language task using PCFGs, and extends evaluation to language models to gain insights into linguistic structure.

The paper frames a methodology to characterize and evaluate FIDAMs, including formal-language tasks as a grey-box evaluation setup for faithfulness in linguistic structure learning by LMs.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: This candidate directly targets the core question of whether language models encode and reveal syntactic structure, using Transformer-based NLP (RoBERTa on CoLA) and formal-language tasks to probe grammar knowledge via FIDAMs. While formal-language experiments include LSTMs, the presence of Transformer-based NLP experiments and explicit discussion of linguistic structure in language models suffice to treat this as a topical, evidence-based contribution under the original Stage 2 criteria. Minor uncertainties arise from the distribution of Transformer vs. non-Transformer usage in the formal-language experiments, but the overall content aligns with the Stage 2 goal of empirically analyzing syntactic knowledge in LMs and provides concrete, testable evidence. title: Reconstruction Probing

satisfied_inclusion_points: Uses Transformer-based language models (BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT) and empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge in Transformer LMs.

Parses sentences with a dependency parser to identify syntactic relations and uses MNLI premises (10K) as data for analysis, ensuring non-pretraining-domain context.

evidence_highlights: Abstract: Reconstruction probing, a new analysis method for contextualized representations based on reconstruction probabilities in masked language models.

Abstract: Gains are largely attributable to static and positional embeddings at the input layer.
The paper shows that reconstructability is higher for tokens in subword or head-dependent relationships and that reconstruction boosts depend on syntactic relations.
Ablation analyses show that most gains come from input lexical+positional embeddings rather than full contextualization.

satisfied_inclusion_points: Uses Transformer-based language models (BERT and GPT-2) and empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge via a targeted property-removal framework (TreeDepth and TopConstituents).
Demonstrates that removal of syntactic properties significantly reduces brain alignment across LM layers, providing direct evidence of syntax-related information in Transformer models.
Identifies syntactic properties (TopConstituents and TreeDepth) as the most influential for the brain-LM alignment trend across layers, with effects observed across language ROIs.
Employs a voxelwise fMRI encoding approach with real brain data (Narratives dataset across 18 participants) to link LM representations to brain responses.
Replicates the approach on GPT-2 in addition to BERT, supporting generalization of the syntactic knowledge effect across Transformer models.
uncertain_points: Generalization to languages other than English or to stimuli beyond the Narratives dataset is not addressed in this work.

The property-removal method may partially remove correlated information; the authors note this limitation and compare with INLP, but residual confounds could affect interpretation of causality between syntax and brain alignment.
evidence_highlights: We remove linguistic properties from the pretrained BERT representations, compute residuals, and assess brain prediction performance with a voxelwise encoding model; removal of the linguistic property leads to significant decreases in brain alignment across layers.

The syntactic properties (Top Constituents and Tree Depth) have the highest effect on the trend of brain alignment across BERT layers, indicating these properties are especially crucial for aligning model representations with brain data.
Top Constituents is responsible for the bump in brain alignment in the middle layers for all language regions, while Tree Depth affects temporal and frontal language regions (ATL/PTL and IFG/MFG).
Results are shown not only for BERT but also replicated with GPT-2, suggesting the findings generalize across Transformer-based models.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: This study provides direct empirical evidence linking syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models to brain alignment, addressing the exact topical question of Stage 2 criteria. It uses Transformer models (BERT and GPT-2), a clear empirical analysis of syntactic properties (Top Constituents, Tree Depth), and brain-imaging data to demonstrate a causal-like effect: removing syntax reduces brain alignment across layers. The work also reports ROI- and subregion-level patterns consistent with syntactic processing in the brain. While there are acknowledged limitations (language scope, potential feature confounds), the evidence strongly supports the Stage 2 criteria and represents a core topical evidence-base candidate.

title: Injecting structural hints: Using language models to study inductive biases in language learning

source_record_provenance.record_title: Injecting structural hints: Using language models to study inductive biases in language learning

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses a Transformer-based language model (GPT-2-small) as the base architecture.
The study empirically analyzes syntactic structure by pretraining on formal languages that encode recursion (NEST) and non-context-free crossing dependencies (CROSS).
The study measures downstream language learning performance (perplexity) after fine-tuning on three typologically distant natural languages (English, Japanese, Basque).
The study directly compares recursive versus non-context-free inductive biases to study syntactic inductive biases, showing CROSS biases yield better downstream performance than NEST.
The study includes Zipfian vocabulary distribution bias experiments and shows Zipfian pretraining improves language learning even when pretraining and finetuning vocabularies are unrelated.
uncertain_points: Whether the paper demonstrates direct evidence about the internal syntactic representations within the Transformer models (beyond downstream perplexity) or primarily reports performance on language modeling tasks.

The degree to which the original Stage 2 criteria's demand for explicit analysis of syntactic knowledge is met by the presented formal-language pretraining experiments without additional probing of internal representations.
evidence_highlights: Title and abstract emphasize injecting structural hints and inductive biases into language models to study inductive biases in language learning.

Abstract states three inductive biases investigated: recursive/hierarchical processing, non-context-free crossing dependencies, and Zipfian vocabulary distribution; claims non-context-free interactions form the strongest inductive biases.

Full text describes Experiment 1 (CROSS vs NEST) showing CROSS is a better inductive bias than NEST, Experiment 2 showing small amounts of CROSS improve downstream perplexity, and Experiment 3 showing Zipfian pretraining biases improve learning; languages tested include English, Japanese, Basque.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate directly targets Transformer-based language models and syntactic structure through controlled, empirical manipulations of inductive biases (NEST vs CROSS) and downstream language learning measurements across multiple languages. The work provides concrete evidence on how non-context-free structural biases influence language learning performance, aligning with the Stage 2 criteria for topical evidence-base on syntactic knowledge in LMs. Although it centers on performance metrics (perplexity) and structured pretraining, these are tightly linked to syntactic structure learning, and the cross-linguistic evaluation strengthens its topical relevance. Overall, this work constitutes a core topical evidence-base under the original Stage 2 criteria.

title: BenchCLAMP: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Syntactic and Semantic Parsing

source_record_provenance.record_title: BenchCLAMP: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Syntactic and Semantic Parsing

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study empirically evaluates Transformer-based language models (e.g., T5-base/large/3B, BART-large, CodeT5-base, GPT-3, Codex, Llama-2) on syntactic and semantic parsing tasks, directly addressing syntactic knowledge in LMs.

It reports performance on syntactic parsing tasks (PTB-3 constituency parsing; UD-EWT dependency parsing) and on multiple semantic/parsing tasks (SMCalFlow, TreeDST, MTOP, Overnight, Spider, CoSQL), demonstrating extensive empirical analysis related to syntax and parsing.

The work introduces grammars (context-free grammars) to constrain model outputs to valid representations, enabling controlled evaluation of syntactic/semantic parsing capabilities in Transformer-based LMs.

Results show the impact of constraints and context on parsing performance, including findings relevant to syntactic knowledge under low-resource and high-resource regimes, aligning with the criteria's emphasis on empirical assessment of syntactic structure in LMs.
evidence_highlights: BenchCLAMP introduces context-free grammars for nine parsing datasets (seven semantic, two syntactic) and a constrained decoding interface to generate only valid outputs, enabling empirical evaluation of LM parsing.

The study evaluates transformer-based LMs (T5, BART, GPT-3, Codex, Llama-2, etc.) on a suite of syntactic and semantic parsing tasks, reporting dataset-specific metrics (Lispress match, EVALB LAS, Smatch, etc.).

Grammars are released for all datasets to constrain generation to valid meanings; constrained decoding is shown to be essential for few-shot prompting and for tasks with complex constraints like constituency and dependency parsing.

Results across SMCalFlow, TreeDST, MTOP, Overnight, Spider, and CoSQL demonstrate empirical analysis of syntactic/semantic parsing abilities in Transformer-based models, with grammar-constrained decoding impacting performance, especially in low-resource settings.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: BenchCLAMP provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation of Transformer-based language models on syntactic parsing tasks (e.g., PTB-3, UD-EWT) and related semantic parsing tasks, using context-free grammars to enforce valid outputs and analyzing constrained decoding across multiple models and data regimes. This directly aligns with the Stage 2 criteria of examining syntactic knowledge in Transformer models and offers a substantive, evidence-based topical contribution. There is no evidence to suggest exclusion; the work is a direct topical evidence-base candidate under the original Stage 2 criteria, hence a core role.

The analysis by phenomenon reveals that Transformer models perform well on local dependencies but struggle with long-distance dependencies such as verbal agreement and binding.

evidence_highlights: How Well Do Text Embedding Models Understand Syntax?

Text embedding models have significantly contributed to advancements in natural language processing by adeptly capturing semantic properties of textual data. However, the ability of these models to generalize across a wide range of syntactic contexts remains under-explored.

We first develop an evaluation set, named SR, to scrutinize the capability for syntax understanding of text embedding models from two crucial syntactic aspects: Structural heuristics, and Relational understanding among concepts.
Sentence-T5, which is trained on a large scale of web-based question-answering data, demonstrates most robust performance.
2.1 Foundation Corpus for SR Construction ... STS, SICK, CQADupStack, Twitter, BIOSSES, AskUbuntu.

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study explicitly investigates Transformer-based language models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) and their capacity to parse via the Inside-Outside algorithm on English PCFG data.
It empirically analyzes syntactic structure in LM representations by recovering parse trees and marginal span probabilities from pre-trained models on PCFG-generated data.
It demonstrates that the Inside-Outside algorithm yields the optimal MLM loss on PCFG-generated data (Theorem 3.3).
It provides theoretical constructions showing that Transformers can simulate the Inside-Outside algorithm (Theorems 3.1 and 3.2) and discusses size reductions in Section 3.3.

It includes probing experiments (Section 4) showing parse information is encoded in intermediate states and that probes can predict marginal probabilities, indicating syntactic knowledge in LM representations.

It reports parsing performance and analysis (e.g., 71.33% sentence F1 with reduced head counts in Table 2) and discusses the role of non-terminals/PCFG structure in enabling parsing within transformers.
It explicitly links MLM training to parsing capabilities on PCFG data, connecting syntactic information to the MLM objective (Section 3.2).
uncertain_points: The evaluation is conducted on synthetically generated PCFG data rather than natural language sentences; generalization to real-world natural language parsing remains to be validated.
The scope is demonstrated with RoBERTa/BERT on English PCFG; broader cross-model and cross-language validation would strengthen generalization.
While the results show syntactic information in intermediate states, full generalization to broad syntactic phenomena across diverse corpora could benefit from additional experiments.
evidence_highlights: The abstract states: 'we show that masked language models like BERT or RoBERTa of moderate sizes can approximately execute the Inside-Outside algorithm for the English PCFG' (direct topical claim).
Theorem 3.1 (Hard attention) and Theorem 3.2 (Relative positional embeddings) show explicit transformer constructions that simulate the Inside-Outside algorithm across spans and non-terminals.
Theorem 3.3 asserts that Inside-Outside achieves the optimal MLM loss under PCFG-generated data, linking parsing and MLM optimization.

Section 4 presents probing results: high correlation between probe outputs and marginal probabilities computed by Inside-Outside, across PCFG, PTB, and OOD settings (evidence of syntactic information in LM representations).

Table 2 demonstrates that with a restricted set of frequent non-terminals and transformations, the model achieves substantial parsing performance (e.g., 71.33% sentence F1) while reducing heads, illustrating practical feasibility.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate directly addresses Transformer-based language models and syntactic knowledge via an empirical and theoretical program around the Inside-Outside algorithm on PCFG data, with probing evidence showing parse information in LM representations and MLM loss alignment. Uncertainties mainly concern generalization to natural language beyond PCFG-generated data; these do not undermine the core topical relevance but are noted as limitations for broader applicability. evidence_highlights: Title: Neural Networks as Cognitive Models of the Processing of Syntactic Constraints

Abstract: The models analyze the agreement errors made by Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and compare them to those of humans. The models include both LM-only and LM+CCG configurations, and training data effects are examined.

域特定分析顯示代碼域與非英語語言等域出現專門的 heads，顯示模型組件在不同語言與域中有專門化的語法知識模式（5.1、5.2、Fig. 10；文中對代碼與非英語域的描述）。
使用 SVD 等方法解釋頭部變換對應的語義概念，提供可解釋性的語法相關映射（5.2、Fig. 11）。
uncertain_points: 雖然以 POS 為核心進行語法相關分析，但未直接提供完整的句法依存分析或系統性的語法知識評估，需評估此證據是否符合原階段 2 對於“分析語法結構或語法知識”的嚴格標準。
該研究的主要焦點在於解釋性分析與信息流路徑抽取，是否能被全部視為原始 Stage 2 標準中的“直接 evidence-base”仍存一定爭議，需要人工判讀是否有遺漏之處。
evidence_highlights: 4.1 Component Importance for POS：使用 POS 標註並透過 t-SNE 對輸入 token 的詞性與模型貢獻的關係進行分群，顯示語法類別影響信息流路徑。
Figure 8：t-SNE 展示以輸入 POS/下一個詞的 POS 著色的組件重要性向量，直觀呈現功能詞與內容詞在不同分類中的表現差異。
4.3 Positional heads 與 Subword merging heads：提出“前一個 token heads”和“子詞合併 heads”在下層到中層均具有普遍重要性，解釋為何某些詞在語法層級具有影響力。
5 Domain-specific Model Components：顯示域特定的 heads 在代碼與非英語語料中具有重要性，證明模型組件具有域特異性。
Figure 11：使用 SVD 對 W_h^OV 進行分解，將頭部轉換投影到未嵌入矩陣，解釋為與語彙概念相關的特定輸出。
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: 本候選文獻在實證層面對 Transformer-based 語言模型進行語法相關分析，透過 POS 基礎分析與語法相關的頭部功能研究，顯示模型在語法知識層面的行為模式具有可觀的可重現性與域特異性。雖然其核心聚焦於信息流路徑與模型解釋性，而非嚴格的句法依存分析，但研究內容與原 Stage 2 criteria 的要求高度吻合：對 Transformer-based LMs 進行了實證分析，並涉及語法相關結構與知識的探討。因此優先判定為 core。但因其證據多以 POS 與資訊流分析為主，尚存在將語法知識定義為“直接的語法結構分析”之爭議，因此在 uncertain_points 中註記需人工判斷是否符合該嚴格層級的完整證據。

title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task

source_record_provenance.record_title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses a Transformer-based language model (Gemma 2B) to investigate syntactic knowledge, satisfying the requirement that the work concerns TLMs.
It empirically analyzes syntactic structure knowledge (subject-verb agreement) in Transformer models, addressing the core inclusion criterion.
The analysis is conducted across two languages (English and Spanish), demonstrating cross-lingual circuit behavior relevant to the criteria.

The work identifies a concrete mechanism (subject-number signal encoded as a direction in the residual stream) and a specific computational path (L13H7 → downstream MLP13) that supports the SVA task in both languages.

The paper provides causal evidence (activation steering using PC1English) that manipulating the identified direction can alter Spanish verb number predictions, showing direct evidential support for the syntactic knowledge mechanism.
evidence_highlights: Gemma 2B is analyzed to study subject-verb agreement circuits, highlighting a language-independent subject-number signal encoded in the residual stream.
Attention head L13H7 and downstream MLP13 are identified as central to propagating the subject-number signal across layers.
Activation patching and direct logit attribution reveal how subject information influences verb form predictions in English and Spanish.
PC1English captures a 1-dimensional subspace encoding subject number; steering Attn13,7 toward PC1English causally flips Spanish verb number predictions.
The study provides cross-language evidence that similar circuit mechanisms underlie SVA in English and Spanish within the same Transformer model.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: This candidate provides direct, empirical evidence relating to the Stage 2 criteria: it investigates syntactic knowledge (SVA) within a Transformer LM (Gemma 2B), provides detailed mechanistic analysis (attention heads, MLP neurons) and causal manipulation (activation steering) across two languages (English and Spanish). The findings—especially the language-agnostic subject-number signal encoded in a residual subspace and its causal influence on predictions—constitute a strong topical evidence base that aligns with the original Stage 2 criteria. Therefore, it should be labeled core as a direct topical evidence-base candidate under criteria_stage2/2601.19926.json.

title: Tree Transformers are an Ineffective Model of Syntactic Constituency

source_record_provenance.record_title: Tree Transformers are an Ineffective Model of Syntactic Constituency

satisfied_inclusion_points: Directly analyzes Transformer-based language models (Tree Transformer / TreeBERT) and uses a Transformer-based architecture.

Empirically analyzes syntactic structure representations by examining latent constituency trees and performing syntactic tasks (e.g., determiner-noun merges, adjective-noun combinations, subject-verb agreement).
Pretrains a Tree Transformer variant (Tree-BERT) and evaluates on in-distribution and generalization settings to assess hierarchical and recursive constructs.

Concludes with explicit results about limited evidence of meaningful syntactic constituency representations and only marginal improvements, aligning with the Stage 2 topical focus on syntactic knowledge in Transformer models.
uncertain_points: Generalization beyond English and beyond artificially generated data remains uncertain; the study notes limitations due to its data and scope.
Latent constituency representations are inferred from weighted attention rather than discrete parses, raising questions about the robustness of the syntactic interpretation.
Only a subset of syntactic phenomena is covered (Det N, adjectives, agreement, etc.); broader syntactic generalization beyond these tasks remains untested.
evidence_highlights: The Tree Transformer model (Wang et al., 2019) uses a modification to the attention mechanism to induce tree hierarchy from input tokens.
We investigate Tree Transformers to study whether they utilize meaningful and/or useful constituent structures.
We pretrain a large Tree Transformer on language modeling in order to investigate the learned constituent tree representations of sentences, finding little evidence for meaningful structures.

In section 5, we evaluate models on the binary classification task of detecting agreement violations; the results show that while the Tree Transformer models may slightly outperform at these tasks, there is little evidence to suggest a meaningful improvement.
Our conclusion: there is little evidence to support Tree Transformer as an effective model of syntactic constituency.
We observe that the breakpoint probabilities ak tend to be very close to 50% at all tokens in the lowest layer, 75% in the second layer, etc., suggesting the learned structure is not strongly biased.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate is a direct empirical study of syntactic structure representations in Transformer-based models (Tree Transformer / TreeBERT), addressing the core question of whether such models encode/manifest syntactic knowledge. The paper provides evidence, including pretraining and targeted syntax tasks, that Tree Transformer yields limited syntactic advantages and may not constitute a robust model of syntactic constituency. These characteristics align with the Stage 2 criteria and the role-mapping policy’s core classification. While there are acknowledged limitations (artificial data, English-only scope), they do not negate its topical relevance as a foundational evidence-base for Transformer-based syntactic interpretation. Therefore, a core role assignment is warranted.

title: Do LLMs learn a true syntactic universal?

source_record_provenance.record_title: Do LLMs learn a true syntactic universal?

satisfied_inclusion_points: Evaluates Transformer-based language models (Gemini Pro, PaLM) on a syntactic universals question (FOFC) using empirical methods.

Provides targeted syntactic analysis with minimal-pairs to assess whether LLMs respect FOFC, including measurements of log-probability differences between FOFC-respecting and FOFC-disrespecting orders.
Covers multiple languages (Hungarian, Basque, Russian, Serbian, German) and reports language-specific results, with statistical significance reported (p-values) for most languages.

Includes discussion on model size and training data thresholds, showing that FOFC learning varies with data availability and not solely with architecture, aligning with the criterion of empirical assessment of syntactic knowledge in LLMs.
Directly uses Transformer-based models and analyzes syntactic structure knowledge, aligning with the original Stage 2 criteria for topical evidence-base regarding LLMs and syntax.
uncertain_points: Basque presents a data-size related challenge; the universality claim across all relevant languages remains contingent on data availability and potential cross-linguistic transfer effects.
While the paper analyzes FOFC in several languages, extending to additional typologically diverse languages would strengthen generalizability of the Stage 2 criteria applicability.

The interpretation of Basque results hinges on training data thresholds; deeper examination of data distributions and data provenance could further confirm whether Basque reflects developmental plausibility or data scarcity rather than model incapacity.
evidence_highlights: The abstract explicitly frames the FOFC as the central syntactic universality tested against LLMs;
The full text describes minimal-pair transformations and a log-probability scoring approach to quantify FOFC adherence (Figures 2-4);
Results show FOFC learned in Hungarian, Russian, Serbian and German, but Basque remains challenging due to data scarcity, with Basque-specific mean penalties and p-values reported;
The discussion connects model data size and model scale to FOFC learning, indicating that universality is not achieved even with large multilingual models under realistic data budgets;
The metadata and fulltext metadata indicate the candidate is a Transformer-based LLM study focusing on syntactic universals, consistent with the Stage 2 topical criteria.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate Do LLMs learn a true syntactic universal? directly targets a syntactic universality (FOFC) in Transformer-based language models and provides empirical evidence through targeted syntactic evaluation across multiple languages. It tests whether modern LLMs respect FOFC, reports statistical results, and discusses data-size and model-size factors impacting syntactic generalization. These elements align with the original Stage 2 criterion (empirical analysis of syntactic knowledge in TLMs) and position the paper as a core topical evidence-base candidate. While Basque results introduce caveats related to data availability, this does not undermine the overall direct topical relevance and the existence of robust, model-led empirical analysis relevant to the Stage 2 question.

title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models Using Minimal Pairs

source_record_provenance.record_title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models Using Minimal Pairs

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (GPT-2 XL) and empirically investigates syntactic knowledge via decoding probing across internal activations (embeddings, last-token representations, attention matrices).
It employs the BLiMP minimal-pairs benchmark to assess grammaticality across 67 tasks covering 12 phenomena (morphology, semantics-syntax interface, syntax).

The methodology is explicit empirical analysis of syntax in Transformer LMs, using a logistic regression classifier on layer-wise activations with 10-fold cross-validation to decode grammatical vs. ungrammatical labels.

Key findings include that grammatical information is captured in the first third of GPT-2 XL layers, with more complex semantics-syntax and morphology requiring deeper layers, and that attention heads contribute in a collective manner to grammatical representations.
The full text provides per-layer analyses (embeddings/hidden states and attention matrices) and discusses how sentence complexity influences the depth required for capturing linguistic features.
uncertain_points: Generalization beyond GPT-2 XL to other Transformer architectures is not directly tested in this study; the primary model analyzed is GPT-2 XL, which may limit broad generalization across all Transformer LMs.
evidence_highlights: GPT-2 XL is a Transformer-based model with 48 contextual layers; 20 attention heads per layer are analyzed (3.2).
Uses BLiMP benchmark: 67 tasks, 12 phenomena, 1,000 sentence pairs per task (3.1, Table 1 context).
Decoding probing: train binary classifiers on layer activations to distinguish grammatical vs ungrammatical minimal pairs (2.2, 3.3, 3.4).
Findings: grammatical information is learned early (first third of layers) and persists but with varying patterns in later layers (4.2.1).
Complex sentence complexity correlates with deeper feature capture (r = 0.58, p < 1e-4) (4.2.2).
Attention heads show weaker morphology capture but collective heads enhance syntactic/semantic representations (4.4).
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate directly addresses the Stage 2 topic: syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models, via an empirical, layer-wise analysis using a minimal-pairs probing approach (BLiMP) on GPT-2 XL. The evidence demonstrates per-layer encoding of grammar, depth-related learning patterns, and attention-based representations, aligning with the original criteria and providing a concrete, topical evidence-base. While the study focuses on a single transformer model (GPT-2 XL) and baselines (ELMo, GloVe), this does not detract from its status as a core topical evidence-base for syntactic knowledge in Transformers, and the findings address the core inclusion criteria without introducing disqualifying exclusions. Therefore, the role is core with high confidence (stage_score 5).

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (e.g., Pythia, Llama-2, Gemma, OLMo, Mistral) across sizes and training regimens.
It empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge via grammaticality judgments and grammar-related evaluation (BLiMP and minimal pairs based on Dentella et al.).
It explicitly compares methods that probe syntax (production vs forced choice; metalinguistic judgment vs probability) and reports how task demands affect grammar-related performance.

It includes direct measurement of word- and grammar-related probabilities (log probabilities for final words; grammaticality judgments) across multiple LM families, demonstrating syntactic knowledge being tested empirically.

The paper covers grammaticality judgment and syntax-related evaluation within a broad LM-evaluation framework, providing evidence of syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based models under different evaluation paradigms.
uncertain_points: Uncertainty about whether the primary contribution centers on syntactic knowledge analysis itself versus broader evaluation methodology; grammar tests are used but may be secondary to the main theme of task demands.

Generalizability of grammar findings across languages and beyond the tested LM families remains to be further established.
evidence_highlights: Uses BLiMP and Dentella minimal-pair data to evaluate grammatical abilities of multiple Transformer-based models.
Demonstrates a measurable 'demand gap' in grammar-related tasks that shrinks as model size increases or training progresses.
Compares direct probability measurement versus metalinguistic prompts in grammar tasks, showing direct measures often capture grammar knowledge not revealed by metalinguistic prompts.
Shows two evaluation contrasts (production vs forced choice; metalinguistic judgment vs probability) across analogical reasoning, reflective reasoning, word prediction, and grammaticality judgments.
Models evaluated include diverse families (Pythia, OLMo, Gemma, Llama-2, Mistral) across a range of sizes (e.g., Pythia 1B–70B).
Provides explicit methodological detail on how grammar knowledge is probed in LMs (log probabilities conditioned on prefixes; grammaticality judgments via prompting).
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: Original Stage 2 Criteria require the study to be about Transformer-based LMs and to empirically assess or analyze syntactic structure or syntactic knowledge. The Hu_auxiliary_2024 paper fulfills both: it analyzes Transformer-based LMs across multiple sizes and families and empirically tests syntactic knowledge using grammaticality judgments and related syntax-focused tasks (BLiMP, Dentella minimal pairs). Although a portion of the paper emphasizes evaluation design and task demands, the grammar-related experiments represent direct empirical analysis of syntactic knowledge in LMs. Given the evidence, this paper aligns with the core topical criterion and provides direct evidence-base for syntactic knowledge in Transformer LMs under different evaluation paradigms. Therefore, a core role is warranted, with some caveats noted in uncertain_points about centrality vs. methodology emphasis and generalizability.

satisfied_inclusion_points: Empirically analyzes Transformer-based language models (TLMs) in syntactic processing via surprisal and reading-time data.
Uses the SAP Benchmark with seven distinct English constructions and 2000 participants to enable robust construction- and item-level analyses.
Directly compares Transformer-based surprisal to human data, testing whether surprisal explains syntactic processing across multiple constructions.

Demonstrates that Transformer-based surprisal underpredicts processing difficulty and cannot fully explain relative difficulty among different syntactic ambiguities, addressing cross-construction item-level variance.
Includes Transformer-based models alongside LSTM baselines, providing cross-architecture evaluation relevant to the original Stage 2 criteria.
evidence_highlights: The SAP Benchmark comprises seven distinct English constructions and 2000 participants, enabling high-resolution construction- and item-level analysis of syntactic processing.
The study evaluates surprisal from language models, including a Transformer-based LM, and compares it to human reading-time data.
Two architectures (Transformer and LSTM) are used to derive surprisal estimates, enabling cross-architecture evaluation of surprisal predictions.
Results show that LM surprisal diverges from empirical reading-time data, underpredicting processing difficulty and failing to predict relative difficulty across constructions.
The same participants read all constructions, enabling within-subject comparisons and robust item-level analyses across constructions.
The SAP Benchmark is positioned as a standard yardstick for evaluating quantitative theories of human sentence processing, aligning with the broader goals of analyzing syntactic knowledge in LMs.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: Original Stage 2 criteria require the study to focus on Transformer-based language models (TLMs) and to empirically analyze syntactic structure or knowledge within TLMs. The candidate directly tests Transformer-based surprisal against human syntactic processing data using the SAP Benchmark, which includes seven constructions and a large sample with within-subject design. Although LSTM baselines are included, Transformer-based evaluation is central to the analysis, and the findings directly pertain to syntactic knowledge as captured by Transformer models. The full text provides clear evidence that Transformer surprisal alone does not fully account for syntactic processing, strengthening its status as a core topical evidence-base candidate under the Stage 2 criteria. Therefore, the paper is classified as core (stage_score 4 to reflect strong but not absolute certainty given the presence of non-Transformer baselines in the study).

title: Mission: Impossible Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: The paper analyzes Transformer-based language models (GPT-2) and empirically studies their ability to learn syntactic structures using synthetic languages, aligning with the core Stage 2 focus on TLMs and syntax.

It introduces perturbations of English sentences to create *SHUFFLE, *REVERSE, and *HOP languages (with control counterparts), providing a direct testbed for syntactic knowledge and dependencies in LMs.

The study presents quantitative empirical evaluations (perplexities, surprisal) and qualitative/interpretric analyses (causal abstraction, interchange interventions) to assess syntactic learning in LMs, satisfying the empirical evidence criterion.
Data and setup rely on Transformer-based architectures and the BabyLM dataset, with multiple random seeds to establish robustness and confidence intervals (5 seeds).
The work explicitly discusses tokenization and positional encodings as factors influencing syntactic information recovery, addressing core methodological concerns of how LMs encode syntax.

The Full Text includes multiple experiments (perplexities across training steps, surprisal tests for count-based grammar rules, and causal-intervention analyses) demonstrating direct evidence about syntactic knowledge in Transformer LMs.
evidence_highlights: Title indicates a direct investigation into Transformer-based language models and syntactic knowledge in artificial languages.
Abstract and sections describe synthetic impossible languages (SHUFFLE, REVERSE, HOP) used to probe syntactic learning in GPT-2 small models.
Experiment 1 reports perplexity trajectories across languages, showing that models trained on possible languages learn more efficiently than those trained on impossible ones (Figure 2).
Experiment 2 uses surprisal analyses on count-based grammar rules (HOP languages), showing differential learning signals across NOHOP, TOKENHOP, and WORDHOP variants.

Experiment 3 employs causal-abstraction/interchange interventions to identify causal representations related to subject–verb agreement, illustrating how information about markers flows through layers (IIA results in Figure 5).

The Discussion emphasizes that GPT-2 can learn some syntactic patterns but does not master all synthetic impossible languages, challenging broad claims about LLMs’ inability to distinguish possible vs impossible languages.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate is a direct topical fit for Stage 2: it empirically investigates syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models using a carefully constructed set of synthetic languages, with rigorous quantitative and interpretability-based analyses. The evidence clearly aligns with the original Stage 2 criteria (Transformer LMs, empirical syntactic analysis, and an explicit methodology to test syntactic learning). There is no clear exclusion or misalignment; thus, the paper should be labeled core. Minor methodological details (e.g., focus on synthetic languages) reinforce rather than weaken its status as a topical evidence-base candidate for the Stage 2 question about syntactic knowledge in LMs.

It explicitly targets cognitive properties related to syntax: syntactic bias, parsing strategy, and working memory limitations, as described in the Cognitively-motivated LMs section.

It reports global/local correlations between word-order frequencies and negative perplexities, showing that cognitively-motivated LMs align more with typological universals than standard LMs, which directly supports the topical question of syntactic knowledge and its relation to universals.

evidence_highlights: We examine 23 types of uni-directional LMs, which adopt subwords split by byte-pair-encoding (Sennrich et al., 2016) and are trained for 10 epochs.

Under a particular word order configuration o, they jointly predict tokens xo and their syntactic structures yo by incrementally predicting parsing actions ao, such as “NT(S) NT(NP) GEN(I) REDUCE(NP)...”.
PLMs are the same as standard LMs except that they are trained on the action sequences a.
We train an LM on each corpus with word order o and measure the PPL of tokens xo in the respective held-out set.
6.1 Results: The TD and LC variations of the Transformer, LSTM, SRN, and N-gram LMs correspond to the PLMs with their respective architecture.
Most LMs beat the chance rate: Overall, most global and local correlations were higher than the random baseline.

7.1 {S,O,V} word-order biases: Even our cognitively-motivated LMs did not overcome this limitation; the paper notes that the human-like agent-first bias remains unexplained by surprisal-based measures.

evidence_highlights: Unveiling Linguistic Regions in Large Language Models

Furthermore, this core region exhibits significant dimensional dependence, perturbations to even a single parameter on specific dimensions leading to a loss of linguistic competence.

Moreover, we discover that distinct monolingual regions exist for different languages, and disruption to these specific regions substantially reduces the LLMs' proficiency in those corresponding languages.
Freezing the core linguistic region during further pre-training can mitigate the issue of catastrophic forgetting (CF).
We utilize LLaMA-2-7B/13B as our model instance.

title: Learning Syntax Without Planting Trees: Understanding Hierarchical Generalization in Transformers

source_record_provenance.record_title: Learning Syntax Without Planting Trees: Understanding Hierarchical Generalization in Transformers

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study concerns Transformer-based language models and analyzes syntactic knowledge in LMs.

It empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge via hierarchical generalization tasks (e.g., question formation, passivization, tense reinflection, simple agreement) across English and German, with a dedicated generalization test separate from in-distribution data.

The paper demonstrates that the language modeling objective, among five training objectives, consistently yields hierarchical generalization across all tasks, indicating a direct inductive bias relevant to Stage 2 criteria.

It uses decoder-only Transformer models trained from scratch with explicit experimental settings (e.g., 8 heads, embedding dimension 512; 6-layer models; 300k steps; 5 seeds) and synthetic controlled datasets.
The authors propose methods to uncover subnetworks corresponding to different generalizations via attention head pruning and provide a Bayesian interpretation to explain hierarchical generalization.
uncertain_points: While the work provides strong evidence for hierarchical generalization under chosen tasks, it uses synthetic data and a limited set of tasks; the generalizability to broader natural language syntax beyond these tasks is not explicitly demonstrated.

Internal mechanisms of how hierarchical generalization arises within transformer representations are not proven causal; the results show correlation with hierarchical grammar posterior rather than a direct causal demonstration.
The generalization across languages beyond English and German is not explored.
evidence_highlights: Abstract: Transformers trained on natural language data have been shown to exhibit hierarchical generalization without explicitly encoding any structural bias.

Abstract: We extensively experiment with transformers trained on five synthetic, controlled datasets using several training objectives and show that, while objectives such as sequence-to-sequence modeling, classification, etc., often fail to lead to hierarchical generalization, the language modeling objective consistently leads to transformers generalizing hierarchically.

Abstract: We then study how different generalization behaviors emerge during the training by conducting pruning experiments that reveal the joint existence of subnetworks within the model implementing different generalizations.

Abstract: Finally, we take a Bayesian perspective to understand transformers' preference for hierarchical generalization: We establish a correlation between whether transformers generalize hierarchically on a dataset and if the simplest explanation of that dataset is provided by a hierarchical grammar compared to regular grammars exhibiting linear generalization.
Contributions: 'We show that language modeling training objective acts as a source of inductive bias towards hierarchical generalization in transformers.'

Contributions: 'We show that when trained on ambiguous data, transformer LMs learn multiple rules to perform the task that are encoded as subnetworks, which once formed continue to coexist throughout training.'
Contributions: 'Our Bayesian analysis suggests that transformers generalize hierarchically because the hierarchical grammars that fit the data are often “simpler” compared to regular grammars.'
Experiment setup: 'Transformer models from scratch with 8 heads and embedding dimension 512; 6 layers for most tasks; 300k steps; 5 seeds.'
Result: 'Only the language modeling objective consistently obtains high generalization accuracy on all five tasks.'
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: This paper directly tests syntactic knowledge in Transformer language models by evaluating hierarchical generalization across multiple syntactic tasks under a mix of English and German data. It demonstrates that language modeling objectives yield hierarchical generalization where other objectives fail, and it provides analysis of subnetworks and Bayesian explanations, all aligning with the Stage 2 criteria. satisfied_inclusion_points: 研究使用 Transformer-based language models（GPT-2、RoBERTa 等）作為實驗平台，聚焦語言學習中的 Critical Period (CP) 現象。

以實證方式評估語法知識：透過 BLiMP 等語法任務評估模型在 L1/L2 的語法能力，提供直接的語法知識證據，而非僅僅理論探討。

樣本與語言覆蓋相對有限，僅以特定語言對（如英語與德語）以及特定模型（GPT-2/ RoBERTa）為主，未充分展現跨語言與不同架構下的一致性，對於完全符合原條件的廣泛性可能需要更多實驗複現。
雖然使用 BLiMP 與 L1/L2 評估提供語法知識的實證證據，但該測試是否能被直接等同為“Transformer LMs 的語法知識結構/機制的直接證據”仍有待討論，需更清楚地界定這些語法任務與原條件之間的對應程度。
evidence_highlights: 研究聲稱使用語言模型來研究 CP，聚焦於第二語言（L2）與第一語言（L1）流失的 CP 效應。
通過從頭訓練雙語資料、改變對 L2 的暴露年齡，系統地實驗 CP 是否出現在語言模型中。
對模型在 L1/L2 的語法能力進行評估，並以 BLiMP 作為主要的語法知識指標，報告 BLiMP 的表現與變化。
實驗結果顯示，語言模型並不像人類那樣出現 CP 效應，並且可以通過在訓練後期引入正則化（如 EWC）來模擬塑性下降以再現某些現象。
結論部分指出，CP 效應並非自發地由經驗學習所產生，可能需要先天性機制的解釋，或至少需要將塑性下降等機制引入訓練過程。
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: 本候選論文以 Transformer 基礎的語言模型（GPT-2、RoBERTa 等）作為實驗平台，直接測試語法知識的表徵與表現，並以語法任務 BLiMP 及 L1/L2 的語言表現作為實證證據。其實驗設計（從頭訓練、雙語資料、暴露於 L2 的年齡變化、以及後期引入正則化以模擬塑性下降）與原始 Criteria 下對語法知識的研究方向具有直接的實證相關性，且提供了可量化的語法知識證據與 CP 概念的理論啟示。因此，將此論文歸類為 core（直接符合原 Stage 2 條件且為主動的 topical evidence-base），雖然其核心焦點是 CP 而非專注於語法知識的可解釋性分析，但其實驗證據涵蓋 Transformer LMs 的語法知識屬性，且屬於原始條件下的實證證據基礎。

title: Evidence of Generative Syntax in LLMs

source_record_provenance.record_title: Evidence of Generative Syntax in LLMs

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT-2, Qwen) and empirically investigates syntactic knowledge in LLMs.
It empirically assesses syntactic structure in LLMs by applying a dependency-based structural probe (Hewitt & Manning, 2019) to test for generative syntax representations.
The authors construct and analyze a large SR/SC dataset (33,120 unique sentences) with 6 SR verbs and 6 SC verbs, across 8 subjects and 61 embedded verbs, including pronoun and nominal object cases.
The methodology measures hierarchical syntactic distances via word-pair probes (subj-embed, subj-infin, subj-dobj, embed-dobj) to detect differences predicted by generative syntax theories.

Results show significantly longer distances for SC vs SR in subj-embed and subj-dobj across multiple models, aligning with the predictions of generative syntax that SC trees are more complex than SR trees.
uncertain_points: Infinitive 'to' (subj-infin) results are significant only for some models, raising questions about whether this pattern reflects genuine generative syntax or model/semantic factors.
There is variability across models in capturing the SR/SC distinction, which suggests model-dependent effects that may require further cross-model replication.

The probe is dependency-based and probes hierarchical structure indirectly; while informative, it does not reconstruct full generative trees and may conflate semantic effects with syntactic-hierarchical signals.
evidence_highlights: The paper applies Hewitt and Manning's dependency-trained probe to test for theory-backed generative syntactic structures in LLMs.
A dataset of 33,120 SR/SC sentences is generated by pairing 6 SR verbs with 6 SC verbs across 8 subject words and 61 embedded verbs, including pronoun and nominal object variations.
Key word-pairs analyzed are subj-embed, subj-infin, subj-dobj, and embed-dobj, to capture distances that differ under SR vs SC despite identical dependency surface parses.

Across multiple models (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT-2, Qwen families), SC conditions yield longer predicted distances than SR for subj-embed and subj-dobj, consistent with SC’s larger CP complement in generative syntax.
embed-dobj baseline shows no systematic SC/SR difference, supporting the validity of the observed effects for the targeted syntactic distinctions.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: This manuscript directly investigates transformer-based language models and empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge using a structural probe, aligning with the Stage 2 criteria for topical evidence on syntactic representations in LLMs. The core finding—that SC tends to produce longer hierarchical distances than SR in key word-pairs across several models—provides concrete, model-agnostic evidence that LLMs encode deeper hierarchical syntactic structures as posited by generative syntax. While there are model-dependent nuances (notably subj-infin results varying by model) that introduce some uncertainty, these do not overturn the primary evidence, and the study constitutes a strong direct topical evidence-base under the original Stage 2 criteria. Therefore, the paper is categorized as core, with minor uncertainties noted for specific edge cases and model variability. The uncertainties are appropriately captured in uncertain_points for transparent next-step investigation.

title: Evidence of Hierarchically-Complex Syntactic Structure Within BERT’s Word Representations

source_record_provenance.record_title: Evidence of Hierarchically-Complex Syntactic Structure Within BERT’s Word Representations

satisfied_inclusion_points: Paper studies Transformer-based language models (e.g., BERT) and analyzes syntactic knowledge via empirical methods.
Uses a structural probe (based on Hewitt & Manning, 2019) to analyze syntactic structure in contextualized embeddings.
Tests hierarchical syntactic distinctions by manipulating complement sizes (vP, TP, CP) while keeping certain dependencies constant.
Constructs a large dataset (18,252 sentences) covering multiple constructions (BareVP, SingTP, SingCP, DoubTP, DoubCP) to probe constituency depth.
Concludes that BERT representations capture hierarchical syntactic structure, consistent with Minimalist theory, providing direct topical evidence for syntactic knowledge in Transformer LMs.
uncertain_points: Interpretation hinges on a single probe framework; replication across other models or languages would strengthen generalization.
Some results (e.g., DoubTP with small samples) may reflect data sparsity or probe limitations; broader validation could reduce over-interpretation of specific interactions.
evidence_highlights: The study provides empirical support that LLMs’ contextualized word embeddings have captured deep and hierarchical syntactic structure.
It extends Hewitt & Manning’s 2019 structural probe to test for variations in constituency depth (vP vs TP vs CP) under Minimalist analyses.
The authors designed 18,252 sentences where dependency parses are identical but constituency trees differ due to complement size (vP/TP/CP).
Results show CP-level embeddings yield longer projected distances than VP/TP embeddings, and interactions with linear distance indicate sensitivity to constituency size.

Discussion notes that pretrained models like BERT may have learned representations approximating hierarchical distinctions between different complement sizes, suggesting constituency representations may be learned “for free” within dependency-based probes.
The work argues that if models implicitly learn constituency representations, it may reduce the need for explicit, dense constituency grammars in NLP systems.

title: Probing Internal Representations of Multi-Word Verbs in Large Language Models

source_record_provenance.record_title: Probing Internal Representations of Multi-Word Verbs in Large Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: Uses a transformer-based language model (BERT) and empirically analyzes internal representations of syntactic knowledge in LMs (e.g., phrasal vs. prepositional verbs).
Employs probing classifiers (token-level and sentence-level) across layers to measure linguistic information and layer-wise distribution of syntax.
Applies Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV) to assess data separability of verb-category representations across layers.
Uses a linguistically motivated dataset (BNC-based) with training and test splits for phrasal and prepositional verbs, ensuring non-overlap between training and test sets.

Demonstrates that middle layers capture linguistic distinctions; discusses limitations of probing and non-linear representations, aligning with interpretability literature on syntactic knowledge in transformers.
evidence_highlights: Model: bert-base-uncased used as the feature extraction LM; 12 layers; 768-dim representations across layers (2.2 Model).
Probing classifiers (Logistic Regression, Linear SVM) trained on BERT activations to classify phrasal vs. prepositional verbs at token and sentence levels (2.3 Classification Models; 3 Results).
GDV analysis used to quantify cluster separability across layers, reporting near-zero to mildly negative values with peak separability in early/mid layers (3. GDV Values).
Dataset construction: training set with 1920 phrasal and 2070 prepositional verbs; test set with 522 phrasal and 623 prepositional verbs; citable in Table 1 and Methods (2.1 Data).

Findings indicate middle layers (approx layers 5–7 for sentence-level, 6–9 for token-level) are most informative for syntactic distinctions, consistent with layer-wise linguistic representation literature (3. Results).

Discussion acknowledges limitations of probing and non-linear representations, aligning with interpretability findings in the literature and providing a balanced view of how syntactic knowledge is distributed in transformer representations.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate directly interrogates syntactic representations in a transformer-based LM (BERT) using empirical probing methods across layers to distinguish two morphosyntactic categories of multi-word verbs. It employs a linguistically motivated dataset, clear empirical tasks (token- and sentence-level classifications), and interpretable metrics (GDV) to map where syntactic knowledge resides in the model. This aligns with the Stage 2 criteria for topical evidence-base on syntactic knowledge in LMs and constitutes a direct evidence-base study rather than a background or protocol piece. Therefore, it should be labeled core.

source_record_provenance.record_title: Targeted Syntactic Evaluation for Grammatical Error Correction

satisfied_inclusion_points: The paper explicitly references Transformer-based language models as part of its GEC evaluation (Transformer category described in 4.1).

triggered_exclusion_points: The original Stage 2 criteria emphasize a study about Transformer-based language models with explicit empirical assessment or analysis of syntactic structure or syntactic knowledge within TLMs. While CTSEG uses Transformer-based models for evaluation, its primary emphasis is dataset construction and model-agnostic evaluation methodology rather than a direct analysis of syntactic knowledge or interpretability within Transformer networks themselves.

CTSEG situates its contributions largely as a dataset/evaluation framework for GEC rather than a study focused on the internal representations or interpretability of Transformer LMs, which may limit its alignment with the core intent of the Stage 2 criteria as originally defined.
uncertain_points: Whether the CTSEG paper should be treated as a direct criteria-grounded analysis of Transformer-based syntactic knowledge (bocusing on internal representations/interpretability) or primarily as a targeted evaluation dataset for LM-based GEC models.

To what extent the evidence qualifies as a 'topical evidence-base candidate under those criteria' given that the main contribution is dataset design and evaluation methodology rather than a rigorous interpretability/syntactic analysis of Transformer models.
Whether more explicit alignment with the 'the Grammar of Transformers' interpretability focus would be required for a stronger core classification.
evidence_highlights: Title: Targeted Syntactic Evaluation for Grammatical Error Correction
Abstract: proposes a Targeted Syntactic Evaluation dataset (CTSEG) and evaluates three mainstream GEC model types (sequence-to-sequence, sequence tagging, and prompt-based) across grammar items.

Full text: 4.1 Transformer describes transformer-based model as part of the GEC models evaluated; 3.2 Grammar Items List notes 263 CEFR-J grammar items; 3.3 Post-processing to M2; 4.2 Individual Scores and 4.4 Recall per grammar item illustrate empirical analysis of syntactic-item performance.
Section 5: Leveraging GPT-4 to Support Language Learners demonstrates targeted recall evaluation and prompt-controlled corrections, reinforcing the focus on syntactic-item level performance.
The CTSEG methodology (minimal pairs per grammar item, CEFR-aligned items, M2 formatting) provides an empirical basis for evaluating syntactic knowledge as manifested by LM-based models.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: CTSEG demonstrates empirical evaluation of syntactic-item performance across language models, including Transformer-based ones, via a targeted syntactic evaluation framework. However, its primary contributions are dataset design and evaluation methodology for GEC rather than an explicit, in-depth analysis of Transformer internal syntactic representations or interpretability. Therefore, it aligns more with a bridging role (bridge) than a definitive core topical anchor for Stage 2 criteria, though it provides substantial evidence related to syntactic evaluation of Transformer-based LMs. The classification reflects this partial alignment and notes the need for manual review to confirm strict criterion-compliance.

title: Sneaking Syntax into Transformer Language Models with Tree Regularization

source_record_provenance.record_title: Sneaking Syntax into Transformer Language Models with Tree Regularization

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study focuses on Transformer-based language models (transformer LMs) and investigates syntactic knowledge.
It empirically analyzes syntactic structure/knowledge in LMs using a differentiable regularizer (TREEREG) and Span Contextual Independence Score (SCIN).

The work provides direct empirical evaluation on syntactic generalization benchmarks (BLiMP, SyntaxGym [SG]), including quantitative improvements (e.g., up to 9.5 points on SG) and parsing-related metrics (unlabeled F1 ~90 on multiple datasets).
It demonstrates that TREEREG can induce tree-like structure in transformer LMs and aligns induced parses with gold or silver parses (high F1 scores on BLLIP-LG, PTB, and 4kQ).

The full text presents concrete experimental results across multiple model scales (from base LMs to large LLMs) and tasks, evidencing direct topical relevance to syntactic knowledge in Transformer LMs.
uncertain_points: Generalization across languages beyond English is not demonstrated; most evidence centers on English corpora (BLiMP, SG, BLLIP-LG/PTB).
While syntactic generalization improves, the long-term impact on broader interpretability questions or downstream tasks beyond syntactic tests is not exhaustively covered.
evidence_highlights: TREEREG introduces a differentiable loss that biases transformer circuits toward hierarchical structure by maximizing Span Contextual Independence Score (SCIN) for constituent spans and minimizing it for non-constituent spans.
The paper reports up to 9.5 points improvement on SG (SyntaxGym) and 2.6 points on BLiMP when TREEREG is applied, with maintained or improved perplexities in several settings.
Unlabeled F1 scores against parses on BLLIP-LG/PTB/4kQ datasets are near or above 90 for TREEREG models, indicating strong induced parsing capabilities.

TREEREG enables parsing of induced trees across layers, showing increasing alignment with given parses up to a mid-layer and then a decline, suggesting a distinct syntactic representation evolving through the network.

The approach preserves transformer architecture (no architectural changes), adds auxiliary loss during training, and works with parsed data or mixed parsed/unparsed data, highlighting practical applicability.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate directly addresses the Stage 2 topic—investigating syntactic knowledge within Transformer-based language models—via empirical methods and benchmarks. It introduces a novel, differentiable regularizer (TREEREG) that enforces hierarchical structure in transformer representations and provides robust evidence (SCIN-based analysis, high parsing F1, and substantial syntactic generalization gains on BLiMP, SG) across multiple model scales and datasets. The evidence aligns with core criteria for topical evidence-base within the original Stage 2 scope, and there are no clear exclusion signals. Given the depth of empirical demonstration and direct relevance to syntactic knowledge in LMs, the work is best classified as core.

title: Derivational Probing: Unveiling the Layer-wise Derivation of Syntactic Structures in Neural Language Models

source_record_provenance.record_title: Derivational Probing: Unveiling the Layer-wise Derivation of Syntactic Structures in Neural Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (BERT-base and BERT-large) to study syntactic knowledge (Section 5.2).

It empirically analyzes syntactic structures (micro- and macro-syntactic) across layers using a Derivational Probing framework that combines structural probing with an expected layer metric (Section 4).
It uses UUAS as a metric to quantify syntactic structure across layers (Section 3.2).
The results indicate a bottom-up derivation: micro-syntactic structures emerge in lower layers and macro-syntactic structures emerge in higher layers (Section 6.2).
A targeted subject-verb agreement analysis shows the timing of macro-syntactic integration affects downstream performance (Section 7).
The full text uses WikiText-103 data and spaCy for dependency parsing to construct the syntactic structures analyzed (Section 5.1, 5.2).
The work contributes to interpretability of syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models (overall framing and conclusions).
uncertain_points: Generalizability to transformer architectures beyond BERT-base/large is not demonstrated (results reported for two BERT variants only).
English-language data only (no multilingual analysis) limits cross-language generalizability.
Potential semantic confounds of syntactic probing are not exhaustively controlled (discussion of semantics vs. syntax is limited).
Dependency-parsing-based evaluation may bias results toward parse-centric notions of syntax; broader syntactic theories are not tested.
evidence_highlights: BERT-base and BERT-large are analyzed across all layers (Section 5.2).
Derivational Probing merges structural probing with the expected layer metric to track micro- and macro-syntactic subgraphs across layers (Section 4).
Macro-syntactic structures show higher expected layers than micro-syntactic ones, suggesting bottom-up construction (Figure 4, Section 6.2).
Subject-verb agreement analysis demonstrates the importance of the timing of macro-syntactic integration for downstream performance (Section 7).
BERT-base achieves 984/1000 grammatical sentences in a controlled S-V task; BERT-large achieves 983/1000 (Section 7.1).
MDS visualizations illustrate the evolution of syntactic representations across layers (Section 7.2).
The method and results are framed as an interpretability study of syntactic knowledge in Transformer models (Abstract and Conclusion).
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate directly tackles the Stage 2 topical question about interpretability and syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models. It provides empirical evidence (across two BERT variants) of how syntax is constructed across layers, leveraging a novel Derivational Probing framework, and reports concrete results (micro vs macro syntactic structure timing, UUAS across layers, and S-V agreement analyses). This aligns with the original Stage 2 criteria (topic S1; empirical analysis of syntactic structure in TLMs). Therefore, it should be labeled core with high confidence, while noting some limitations in generalizability to other architectures/languages which could be addressed in future work (hence stage_score 4).

- It includes analysis of how memory size and plugin configurations affect performance (e.g., memory size effects, ablation across C/D/S knowledge types) and presents a case study illustrating how the plugin weights align with informative syntactic dependencies.

- While there is some analysis of the plugin's weighting of dependencies (case study), there is no direct disclosure of internal Transformer-level representations of syntax; assessment relies on external memory modules and their impact on output, which may require human vetting to confirm full topical alignment with the original criteria.
evidence_highlights: - Abstract: "we propose an approach that integrates extendable components capable of incorporating various types of syntactic knowledge, such as constituent syntax, word dependencies, and combinatory categorial grammar (CCG). Importantly, this encoder acts as a versatile, detachable plugin that is trained independently of the LLM. We conduct experiments on benchmark datasets, which show that our approach outperforms strong baselines and previous approaches, thus demonstrates its effectiveness."

It takes the input text (which includes X and A) and a list of key vectors K and a list of value vectors V, and produce a vector that encodes the knowledge... the weighted sum of the value embeddings and obtain the output oP of the plugin"

Remaining uncertainties relate to how directly this maps to interpretability of the transformer's internal representations, and whether the alignment with the specific interpretability framing of the original criteria should be treated as a close but not perfect fit; however, the substantive evidence supports a core classification with caveats noted in uncertain_points.

title: Extracting structure from an LLM - how to improve on surprisal-based models of Human Language Processing

source_record_provenance.record_title: Extracting structure from an LLM - how to improve on surprisal-based models of Human Language Processing

satisfied_inclusion_points: Uses a Transformer-based language model (GPT-2) and an automatic parser (spaCy) to empirically analyze syntactic structures of subphrases predicted by the model.
Conducts an empirical study (garden-path sentences, self-paced reading times) to test the relationship between model-derived structure distributions and human processing data.

Demonstrates that structure-informed measures (Incompatibility Fraction, IFmin/IFJS) correlate with human reading times and outperform surprisal in predicting reading-time differences between garden-path conditions (NP/S vs NP/Z).
Directly targets Transformer-based LMs and syntactic knowledge with an empirical evaluation, aligning with the Stage 2 criteria for topical evidence-base on syntactic knowledge in LMs.
uncertain_points: While the work analyzes syntactic structure using model-generated continuations and external parses, it relies on external parsing (spaCy) to obtain grammatical structures rather than exclusively internal model representations; further work could clarify to what extent the findings reflect internal syntactic representations within GPT-2 vs. downstream parsing abstractions.

The study focuses on a specific experimental paradigm (garden-path sentences) and a particular dataset; generalization to a broader range of syntactic phenomena or other Transformer models beyond GPT-2 would strengthen topical coverage.
The originality vs. replication scope across different LLMs could be explored further to firmly establish Stage 2 role boundaries across the broader transformer-LM landscape.
evidence_highlights: GPT-2 (Transformer) is used as the primary LLM to generate continuations and derive subphrase structures; spaCy provides the grammatical parses, enabling a structure-based analysis of syntax within an LLM pipeline.
IFmin and IFJS are used as structure-aware difficulty measures and are shown to correlate with human reading times (significant Pearson correlations, high values, and strong p-values).
The approach yields regression-based predictions of reading times and differentiates garden-path effects between NP/S and NP/Z, performing better than surprisal (SP) in several metrics.

Results indicate that combining syntactic structure information with probabilistic statistics from an LLM improves alignment with human processing data, supporting the claim that transformer LMs encode usable syntactic information.
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate directly satisfies the Stage 2 criteria: it studies a Transformer-based language model (GPT-2) and empirically analyzes syntactic structure/knowledge, using a rigorous empirical design with human reading-time data to validate model-derived structural measures. It demonstrates that structure-informed metrics correlate with human processing and outperform surprisal in key tasks, making it a strong core/topical evidence-base candidate under the original Stage 2 criteria. The role assignment is confident given the clear direct linkage to syntactic knowledge in LLMs and the empirical emphasis on structure vs. purely statistical surprisal.

title: Can Language Models Learn Typologically Implausible Languages?

source_record_provenance.record_title: Can Language Models Learn Typologically Implausible Languages?

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses Transformer-based language models (GPT-2 and LTG-BERT) to study syntax-related learnability.
It empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge via broad syntactic tests (BLiMP and JBLiMP) and minimal-pair evaluations.
It employs top-down counterfactual corpus manipulations to compare typologically plausible (harmonic) vs implausible languages across English and Japanese.
It reports evaluation results across multiple syntactic benchmarks (BLiMP/JBLiMP) and languages, demonstrating measurable syntactic knowledge-related effects in LMs.
It concludes with findings about harmonic language biases in LMs, directly addressing how syntactic knowledge manifests in Transformer models under typological manipulation.
uncertain_points: The evidence is performance-based on syntactic benchmarks (BLiMP/JBLiMP) rather than direct inspection of internal representations of syntax within the models; this is a common, but notable, interpretive limitation.

Authors acknowledge potential noise from parser errors in counterfactual corpora, which could partly influence results; broader replication across more languages/models would strengthen generalizability.
evidence_highlights: "We test learnability of two types of LMs (autoregressive and masked) from scratch on each of our counterfactual languages. We evaluate learnability from multiple perspectives: (i) perplexity per token on the entire corpus, (ii) preferences on minimal pairs targeting the manipulated feature; and (iii) broad syntactic tests (BLiMP, Warstadt et al., 2020; and JBLiMP, Someya and Oseki, 2023)."
"Our experimental results show that LMs often struggle to learn counterfactual, typologically implausible languages relative to minimally different natural languages."
"Figure 4 shows the performance trajectories of English-based counterfactual LMs in BLiMP (left) and Japanese-based counterfactual LMs in JBLiMP (right)."

"These findings lend credence to the conclusion that LMs do show some typologically-aligned learning preferences, and that the typological patterns may result from, at least to some degree, domain-general learning biases."
stage2_role_review.decision_rationale: The candidate directly addresses Transformer-based LMs and empirically evaluates syntactic knowledge using established syntactic benchmarks (BLiMP/JBLiMP) under a top-down counterfactual language paradigm that manipulates typological harmony. This aligns with the original Stage 2 criteria, making it a core topical evidence-base candidate rather than background or methodological/prov inclusion. While there are acknowledged limitations (noise due to parser errors and limited language/model scope), these do not override the primary, criteria-driven evidence that the paper investigates syntactic knowledge in LMs. Hence, a strong core classification is warranted.

evidence_highlights: Tokenization is a necessary component within the current architecture of many language models, including the transformer-based large language models (LLMs) of Generative AI, yet its impact on the model's cognition is often overlooked.
